lesson_title: How Old Is the Fleet, Really? Fixed Assets and the Auditors
hook_text: Two numbers on a balance sheet can tell you the machines are six years old — and that the business has four years to act.
clip_script: Your uncle hires out bakkies, and his equipment story hides in two numbers anyone can read. The equipment cost one point two million rand, and he writes off a hundred and twenty thousand a year — machinery like this lasts about ten years. The wear account has gathered seven hundred and twenty thousand. Now divide: seven twenty gathered, at one twenty a year — the equipment is SIX years old. Ten-year life, six consumed. Four years left. And four years is not a bookkeeping fact — it is a countdown. A business that waits until year ten meets the replacement bill broke. So the smart owner starts now: a fund, finance, one machine replaced at a time. Then the fleet-wide health check, one comparison: what he ADDED this year against what the year WORE. Added five hundred thousand, wore two ninety — the fleet is getting younger. Flip those numbers year after year and a business is quietly eating itself — and here is the cruel part: the eating years LOOK profitable, because so little is being spent. Plenty of businesses have flattered themselves straight into a dead fleet. Two balance-sheet numbers, one division, one comparison — and you can read any company's future maintenance bill before its own directors admit it.
visual_style: A bakkie depot at dawn; odometer-style counters rolling to show cost and accumulated wear, a big division landing on the number six; a countdown clock over the fleet, then a split-screen of a renewing fleet against a rusting one.
pacing: Two-number setup, satisfying division beat, countdown tension, hard flip to the warning.
call_to_action: Watch the full lesson and read any fixed asset note like a fleet inspector.
